textContent.text: Learning to play music is one of the best decisions you can make! Playing a musical instrument, like the piano or guitar, actually helps your brain. When you practice music, your brain builds new paths between its different parts. These paths help you learn all kinds of things, even math and reading. Learning to play music well also requires you to practice your instrument over and over. All that hard work helps you build discipline and learn to set goals. Not only is playing music good for you, but it's fun, too! You can play songs together with friends, and you can express your inner feelings through music. That's why everyone should start playing music as soon as they can.

textContent.text: Do you have trouble with shoelaces? Well, in 1941, a Swiss inventor named George de Mestral discovered a different way to fasten things. It all began when he went hunting with his dog. After the dog brushed against a burdock plant, de Mestral noticed something. The plant's burrs, or seed pods, were strongly stuck to his dog's fur. De Mestral examined the burrs under a microscope, and he found that each one was covered in tiny hooks. The hooks caught onto loops and tangles in his dog's fur. This allowed the plant to naturally spread its seeds to new places. De Mestral copied this natural design to create Velcro. Today, Velcro brand fasteners are used on shoes, jackets, and even space suits! This amazing invention is just one of many inspired by nature.

textContent.text: Have you seen flamingos at the zoo? They often stand on just one leg. Scientists have different ideas about why they do this.
First, flamingos might lift one leg to stay warm. Their long legs lose heat quickly in cold water, but they stay warmer in the air. By lifting one leg out of the water, flamingos keep that leg warm.

Flamingos might also save energy this way. When flamingos fold one leg against their body, their weight naturally balances above the standing leg. Because of this skill, flamingos can stand for hours using very little energy. They can even stay balanced while asleep!
So, this clever behavior might help flamingos conserve both heat and energy at the same time.

textContent.text: "My lettuce is gone!" Mrs. Torres cried one morning at the community garden. Esperanza listened from her garden patch. She heard other neighbors nodding and saying that their vegetables were missing, too.
It was a mystery! Esperanza knew she needed to look for clues. She knelt and looked at Mrs. Torres' garden beds where vegetables were missing.
Aha! The lettuce leaves were neatly cut, and strange Y-shaped tracks led between the beds.
Esperanza thought about animal prints she knew. "Rabbits!" she told the neighbors.

Some neighbors wanted to keep the rabbits away, but others said animals needed food, too. In the end, everyone worked together to put small wire fences around the vegetables. They also planted extra lettuce outside the new fences for their hungry visitors. Now both the neighbors and the rabbits were happy.

textContent.text: Ice, which is just solid water, floats on top of liquid water. For most other materials, the solid form would sink to the bottom of the liquid. But water acts differently!

The tiny building blocks that are parts of water are called molecules. Water molecules spread out when water freezes into ice. When the water molecules spread out, the ice becomes less dense, or less tightly packed. So, if you have the same volume of ice and water, the ice will be lighter.
This causes ice to float on liquid water. You can see this in any drink with ice, but you may not have known it was so unusual!

"Really?" Yuki asked, touching the smooth rock.
More thunder rolled across the sky. This time, Yuki looked up with curious eyes. "Is the thunder making something beautiful, too?"

textContent.text: It's always surprising to see how a cat twists in the air to land on its feet. This amazing ability is called the righting reflex.

When cats fall, their inner ears tell them which direction is up. Their bendable spines let them twist like a spring. First the front half turns, then the back half follows. This all happens faster than you can blink.

Not only do cats have bendable spines, they also have more of these spine bones than humans. This helps make cats much more bendable than people. They can even twist their front and back halves in different directions.
But cats don't always land safely. They can still get hurt from falls, so it's best to keep pet cats away from dangerous heights.

textContent.text: Carrier pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of miles away, and they almost never get lost. Scientists have discovered that these birds use several clever tricks to know where to go.

For one thing, pigeons have a kind of built-in compass. They can sense Earth's magnetic field, which pulls iron north, and they use it like an invisible map. They also remember landmarks like roads, rivers, and buildings. They follow the same paths each time they travel. Even their sense of smell helps them. Since different places have different scents, pigeons create smell maps to tell them where they are.
Using all these tools, carrier pigeons find home ninety-eight percent of the time. That's why people have used these birds to carry messages for thousands of years.

textContent.text: Do you have trouble with shoelaces? Well, in 1941, a Swiss inventor named George de Mestral discovered a different way to fasten things. It all began when he went hunting with his dog. After the dog brushed against a burdock plant, de Mestral noticed something. The plant's burrs, or seed pods, were strongly stuck to his dog's fur. De Mestral examined the burrs under a microscope, and he found that each one was covered in tiny hooks. The hooks caught onto loops and tangles in his dog's fur. This allowed the plant to naturally spread its seeds to new places. De Mestral copied this natural design to create Velcro. Today, Velcro brand fasteners are used on shoes, jackets, and even space suits! This amazing invention is just one of many inspired by nature.

textContent.text: "My lettuce is gone!" Mrs. Torres cried one morning at the community garden. Esperanza listened from her garden patch. She heard other neighbors nodding and saying that their vegetables were missing, too.
It was a mystery! Esperanza knew she needed to look for clues. She knelt and looked at Mrs. Torres' garden beds where vegetables were missing.
Aha! The lettuce leaves were neatly cut, and strange Y-shaped tracks led between the beds.
Esperanza thought about animal prints she knew. "Rabbits!" she told the neighbors.

Some neighbors wanted to keep the rabbits away, but others said animals needed food, too. In the end, everyone worked together to put small wire fences around the vegetables. They also planted extra lettuce outside the new fences for their hungry visitors. Now both the neighbors and the rabbits were happy.
